title: Adaptive cost-aware routing: GPU class selection + spend-guard enforcement
creator: Marcus Ortega
description:
Objective: Implement an adaptive routing policy that selects between spot and on-demand instances and chooses GPU classes (A100 / H100 / T4 equiv) based on per-customer budget caps, latency tier requirements, and fallback model variants. The feature provides an enforced spend-guard per-customer or per-route, circuit-breaker behavior when budget thresholds are hit, and a preference engine that reasons about GPU throughput, preemption risk, and unit cost for tokens.

Background: Customers increasingly request predictable monthly spend while needing bursty latency-sensitive capacity. Existing soft routing (heuristics in ENG-8421 series) provides cost signals but lacks hard enforcement and fine-grained GPU selection for mixed-capacity fleets. This ticket combines: (1) a deterministic spend guard to prevent runaway spend, (2) a GPU-class scoring function that uses cost-per-token and preemption probability, and (3) automated fallback mapping to cheaper model variants when budget caps are close.

Scope:
- Implement policy evaluation layer in the router that uses customer spend budget and route-level SLOs.
- Add GPU class scoring plugin that consumes kernel-cost profiles to compute expected per-token cost and expected latency.
- Introduce spend-guard actions: throttle (slow-path), downgrade-model, route-to-dedicated (if reserved capacity exists), or reject with graceful error explaining budget hit.
- Expose controls in routing config: budget_cap_monthly, budget_cap_window_seconds, preferred_gpu_classes (ordered), spot_tolerance (0-100), fallback_model_map.

Out of scope: billing invoice changes, long-term quota UI (will be a follow-up), dedicated capacity procurement flows.

Design notes:
- Spend guards live in the smart-router as a local cache of per-customer spend windows (sliding window counters) populated from billing events. To avoid strong coupling with billing, an eventual-consistency model is acceptable: router may conservatively apply caps using high-water marks.
- GPU scoring uses metrics: cost_per_token_estimate, median_latency_ms_for_seq128, preemption_rate_est. We will add a simple exponential-weighted average estimator seeded from benchmarking tables.
- Fallback model mapping: map heavy models to lower-cost variants with preserved semantic profile (e.g., model-x-48k -> model-x-16k-quantized). The mapping will be provided in config by model-onboarding team.

Safety and UX: error responses when budget cap blocks a request must include guidance: remaining budget window, recommended action (upgrade plan, pin to dedicated, or accept lower-quality fallback). For streaming responses ensure fallback is applied before token emission to avoid mid-stream switches.

Acceptance Criteria: see acceptance_criteria field.
acceptance_criteria: Router enforces monthly or sliding-window budget caps for a test customer in staging without billing integration by using simulated spend events.
GPU class scoring influences route selection: when spot and on-demand available, selection aligns with lower expected cost while respecting preemption risk for latency-sensitive routes.
When budget threshold reaches 90% of cap, router automatically applies configured fallback_model_map and returns lower-cost model for new requests.
Spend-guard actions observable in Console: per-customer recent spend, blocked request logs with reasons, and per-route fallback counts.
E2E unit tests for scoring logic, and integration test that simulates spot preemption events and validates fallback or retry behavior.
API errors for budget rejections include structured fields: reason, budget_window_end, suggested_action.
No customer data exfiltration or permission escalation; feature toggled behind 'cost-aware-routing' feature flag.
implementation_notes: Step 1: Add routing policy DSL extension and parser for budget_cap_* and preferred_gpu_classes (router-config module).
Step 2: Implement gpu_scoring service that loads model kernel profiles and recent latency histograms (serving-metrics index).
Step 3: Integrate spend-window cache with billing pubsub; fall back to conservative local estimation if pubsub delayed.
Step 4: Add spend-guard actions with pluggable enforcement (throttle, downgrade, reject).
Step 5: Wire console telemetry endpoints and dashboard panels for spend hits and fallback metrics.
Step 6: Feature-flag rollout through canary on 10% of traffic -> 50% -> 100% with A/B cost/latency monitors.
Estimated engineering work split: router-config 30%, gpu-scoring 25%, spend-cache 20%, observability 15%, QA 10%.
qa_checks: Simulate 1k reqs/min from a test org with small monthly cap and verify router rejects after cap exceeded.
Inject spot preemption events in staging and assert router moves requests to on-demand or fallback model based on route SLO config.
Validate Console shows blocked_request logs with correct structured metadata and links to request traces.
Run load test with heterogeneous GPU fleet and confirm scoring picks GPU classes that reduce expected cost without violating latency SLO for P0 routes.
Security: confirm no billing tokens or PII written into router logs.
Backward compatibility: default routing when fields not present should behave as today (prefer on-demand for low-latency routes).
observability_signals: metric: routing.spend_guard.blocks.count by org_id and reason
alert: sudden increase in spend_guard.blocks (>5x baseline in 1h)
